questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend validating circuit construction on a noiseless simulator before using real hardware?
options: A noiseless simulator run should match the exact theoretically predicted distribution, giving a hard, known-correct check independent of hardware noise
Noiseless simulators are faster than real hardware, which is the only reason given
Real hardware cannot run GHZ circuits at all
Noiseless simulators eliminate the need for zero-noise extrapolation entirely
questions.explain: The lesson explains that a noiseless simulator gives a known-correct theoretical target, so bugs in circuit construction show up immediately -- separate from the queue-time savings, which is a secondary benefit also mentioned.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend testing the zero-noise-extrapolation code on a simulator with an INJECTED, controlled noise model, rather than only a noiseless one?
options: Because you know the true zero-noise answer in advance (since you injected the model), letting you confirm the extrapolation actually recovers it before trusting it on real hardware's unknown noise
Because injected-noise simulators run faster than noiseless ones
Because noiseless simulators cannot execute any circuit with more than one qubit
Because real hardware noise models are identical to injected simulator models
questions.explain: A noiseless simulator has no noise for the extrapolation logic to act on at all, so it can't validate that logic -- an injected, known noise model lets you check the extrapolation against a ground truth you control.

questions.q: What specific data-saving practice does the lesson recommend for diagnosability, rather than saving only the final computed result?
options: Save raw measurement counts per shot batch and per-scaling-factor results before extrapolation, plus device/calibration timestamps
Save only the final extrapolated probability, since intermediate data is never useful
Save only screenshots of the job submission interface
Save nothing until the entire capstone is complete
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly ties diagnosability to keeping intermediate data -- raw counts, per-factor results, and device/calibration info -- so a later discrepancy can be traced to its source, directly connecting to Lesson 9's diagnostic checklist.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say the pipeline should run 3 qubits and then 5 qubits as 'a configuration change, not a rewrite'?
options: Because the capstone proposal requires running the same procedure at two different qubit counts, and code built for one command/one config scales cleanly to both
Because 5-qubit circuits require an entirely different programming language
Because qubit count has no effect on circuit construction
Because rewriting code between conditions is required by the proposal
questions.explain: The lesson's build checklist specifically asks for an end-to-end pipeline that takes qubit count as a parameter, so switching from 3 to 5 qubits for the proposal's planned comparison doesn't require rewriting the pipeline.

questions.q: What is the main reason the lesson gives for always validating experimental code on a simulator before spending real hardware queue time?
options: It catches circuit and analysis bugs against known-correct or known-injected targets, before queue-time-expensive real-hardware runs are used to debug them
Because real hardware access is always free and unlimited, so simulators are only used for style
Because simulators and real hardware always produce numerically identical results
Because real hardware cannot run any circuit without prior simulator validation by policy
questions.explain: The lesson frames simulator-first validation as catching bugs against known targets before using limited, queue-time-costly real hardware runs for debugging -- not as a hard technical requirement imposed by providers.
